lead: Early computers had no operating system. Programmers loaded programs manually using punch cards and toggled switches on the physical machine. As mainframes grew faster and more expensive, idle central processing unit (CPU) time became a costly waste. Operating systems evolved through distinct historical phases—from bare-metal serial processing to simple batch monitors, multiprogrammed batch systems, interactive time-sharing networks, distributed environments, and real-time control systems. Each evolutionary step was invented to solve a specific performance bottleneck, shifting the primary goal from maximizing raw hardware utilization to delivering rapid response times for interactive human users.
prereq: You need to understand basic computer architecture and hardware interrupts from 1.1 Role of an OS and computer-system organization and 1.2 Computer-system architecture and interrupts.

sections.h3: From Bare Machines to Multiprogrammed Batch Systems

blocks.text: In the 1950s, early computers lacked operating systems. A single programmer signed up for a physical block of time on a bare machine, loaded paper tapes or punch cards manually, and ran their program. If the code crashed, the machine stood idle while the user debugged using physical console switches. This mode was called serial processing. Setup times were long, and machine utilization was extremely low.

To reduce setup delay, computer centers introduced simple batch systems in the late 1950s. Operators collected jobs with similar needs from multiple users, grouped them into batches on magnetic tapes, and fed them into a resident program called a monitor. The monitor resided permanently in main memory. When one job finished, the monitor automatically loaded and ran the next job. This introduced job control language (JCL) cards, which told the monitor how to compile, link, and execute the user code.

Simple batch monitors suffered from a severe hardware imbalance: mechanical input/output (I/O) devices like card readers and magnetic tape drives operated in milliseconds, while electronic CPUs operated in microseconds. During an I/O operation, the fast CPU sat completely idle.

To keep the CPU busy, computer architects introduced SPOOLing (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line). Instead of reading cards directly into main memory, a peripheral processor copied input cards to a fast magnetic disk drive. The CPU read input directly from disk and wrote output back to disk. Disk storage acted as a large buffer, decoupling slow peripheral devices from high-speed CPU execution.

SPOOLing enabled multiprogramming. In a multiprogrammed batch system, main memory holds the operating system monitor and multiple user jobs simultaneously. The operating system picks one job from memory and begins executing its CPU instructions. When that job issues an I/O request, the operating system does not let the CPU sit idle. Instead, it switches the CPU to another job in memory that is ready to compute. When the I/O completes, the original job returns to the ready pool.

Multiprogrammed batch systems maximized CPU throughput, but users could no longer interact with their programs while they ran. If a program contained a small syntax error, a programmer waited hours for a printed batch output before fixing a single line of code. To fix this, computer scientists in the 1960s created time-sharing systems (also called multitasking).

Time-sharing extends multiprogramming by using hardware clock interrupts to rapidly switch the CPU among multiple user programs. The operating system assigns each user program a small slot of CPU time, called a time slice or quantum (typically 10 to 100 milliseconds). Because the CPU switches between active programs so quickly, each user connected to a video terminal feels as if they have exclusive access to a dedicated computer.
As computing expanded beyond single mainframes, specialized system types emerged to meet different operational constraints:

items: Distributed Operating Systems: Networked autonomous computers share hardware and software resources over high-speed networks. The user views the entire cluster as a single unified system. Computing loads and data storage are distributed across multiple independent nodes.

Hard Real-Time Systems: Used in critical control environments like anti-lock braking systems (ABS), flight control, or cardiac pacemakers. Every task must guarantee completion within a strict time deadline. Missing a deadline results in immediate physical system failure.

Soft Real-Time Systems: Used in live video streaming, interactive gaming, or online payment gateways like UPI. The system prioritizes critical tasks, but a minor delay or missed deadline degrades service quality without causing catastrophic physical failure.

sections.h3: Contrasting Performance Metrics Across OS Types

blocks.text: Different operating system designs optimize for different performance metrics. Understanding the distinction between these performance indicators is essential for evaluating operating system evolution:

items: Turnaround Time: The total elapsed time from the exact moment a job is submitted to the system until its complete final execution. Batch systems optimize for minimum average turnaround time and maximum system throughput.

Response Time: The time taken from when a user submits a request or presses a key until the system produces the first visible output response. Time-sharing systems optimize for short, predictable response times.

CPU Utilization: The percentage of total time that the CPU is executing useful user or system instructions. Multiprogramming maximizes CPU utilization by overlapping CPU bursts of one program with the I/O bursts of another.

examples.question: Two processes, J1 and J2, enter the system at time t = 0 ms. Each process requires a CPU computation burst of 20 ms followed by an I/O operation burst of 30 ms. Compute the total completion time (in ms) and the CPU utilization percentage under: (a) Uniprogramming (sequential execution), and (b) Multiprogramming (overlapping CPU and I/O bursts).
steps: Step 1: Calculate execution under Uniprogramming (Sequential execution).
J1 runs CPU burst from 0 to 20 ms, then performs I/O from 20 to 50 ms. Total duration for J1 = 50 ms.
J2 starts CPU burst after J1 finishes completely at t = 50 ms. J2 runs CPU burst from 50 to 70 ms, then performs I/O from 70 to 100 ms.
Total elapsed uniprogramming time T_uni = 100 ms.
Total CPU active time = J1 CPU + J2 CPU = 20 ms + 20 ms = 40 ms.
Step 2: Calculate execution under Multiprogramming (Overlapped execution).
At t = 0 ms, J1 starts CPU burst (0 to 20 ms).
At t = 20 ms, J1 releases the CPU to start its 30 ms I/O burst (runs from 20 to 50 ms).
Simultaneously at t = 20 ms, J2 takes the CPU and executes its 20 ms CPU burst (runs from 20 to 40 ms).
At t = 40 ms, J2 finishes its CPU burst and starts its 30 ms I/O burst (runs from 40 to 70 ms).
J1 completes completely at t = 50 ms. J2 completes completely at t = 70 ms.
Total elapsed multiprogramming time T_multi = 70 ms.
Total CPU active time = 20 ms + 20 ms = 40 ms.
examples.answer: Under uniprogramming, the total execution time is 100 ms with a CPU utilization of 40.0%, whereas under multiprogramming, the total execution time drops to 70 ms and CPU utilization increases to 57.14%.
examples.check:
j1_cpu, j1_io = 20, 30
j2_cpu, j2_io = 20, 30
t_uni = j1_cpu + j1_io + j2_cpu + j2_io
util_uni = ((j1_cpu + j2_cpu) / t_uni) * 100
t_multi = max(20 + j1_io, 40 + j2_io)
util_multi = ((j1_cpu + j2_cpu) / t_multi) * 100
print(t_uni)
print(round(util_uni, 2))
print(t_multi)
print(round(util_multi, 2))

traps: Confusing multiprogramming with multiprocessing. Multiprogramming keeps multiple programs in memory to switch CPU execution on a single physical CPU. Multiprocessing uses two or more physical CPUs executing instructions in parallel.

Confusing multitasking (time-sharing) with basic multiprogramming. Basic batch multiprogramming switches jobs only when a running process issues an I/O request or yields. Time-sharing switches processes forcibly using hardware timer interrupts at high frequencies.
Assuming soft real-time systems do not have deadlines. Soft real-time systems have deadlines, but missing a deadline reduces user satisfaction without causing system crashes or physical harm.
Measuring batch operating system performance using response time instead of turnaround time or overall throughput.

quiz.q: What is the primary operational role of SPOOLing in batch processing systems?
quiz.a: SPOOLing uses fast secondary disk storage as a buffer to decouple slow peripheral I/O devices (like card readers) from the high-speed CPU, allowing input/output operations to overlap with CPU execution.

quiz.q: What key distinction separates a hard real-time operating system from a soft real-time operating system?
quiz.a: A hard real-time system guarantees that critical tasks meet strict timing deadlines; missing a deadline causes total system failure. A soft real-time system prioritizes tasks but permits occasional missed deadlines with only a degradation of service quality.

quiz.q: Why did simple batch monitors suffer from extremely low CPU utilization levels?
quiz.a: Simple batch monitors ran only one job at a time. Because I/O devices were mechanical and ran orders of magnitude slower than the electronic CPU, the CPU sat idle waiting for data transfers whenever a job performed I/O.

quiz.q: How does a time-sharing operating system achieve interactive responsiveness for multiple concurrent users?
quiz.a: It uses clock interrupts to switch the CPU rapidly among active user processes in small time slices (quantums). Because switches occur within milliseconds, each user receives prompt feedback, giving the illusion of a dedicated machine.

quiz.q: A system executes 2 jobs sequentially. Job A takes 15 ms CPU and 25 ms I/O. Job B takes 10 ms CPU and 20 ms I/O. Calculate the overall CPU utilization percentage under uniprogramming.
quiz.a: Total elapsed time = (15 + 25) + (10 + 20) = 40 + 30 = 70 ms. Total CPU execution time = 15 + 10 = 25 ms. CPU utilization = (25 / 70) × 100% = 35.71%.

quiz.q: An interactive web server experiences severe response time lag when placed under a traditional batch multiprogramming OS. Analyze why switching to a time-shared OS solves this issue.
quiz.a: In batch multiprogramming, a CPU-bound job holds the CPU continuously until it voluntarily issues an I/O request. Interactive web requests get stuck behind compute-heavy jobs, causing huge response delays. A time-shared OS uses hardware clock interrupts to preempt long CPU-bound jobs after a time slice, giving interactive requests fast CPU access and lowering response time.

quiz.q: Why is a round-robin time-slicing algorithm unsuitable for controlling a missile guidance system?
quiz.a: Round-robin scheduling treats all processes equally by rotating through them in fixed time slices, introducing non-deterministic delay. A missile guidance system is a hard real-time application requiring deterministic priority scheduling with absolute upper bounds on latency to ensure critical sensor inputs are processed immediately.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern operating systems merge these historical modes into hybrid engines. For example, modern Linux servers run soft real-time multimedia workloads alongside interactive time-shared user sessions, while managing distributed container clusters using Kubernetes. Hardware virtualization has transformed OS design by running entire legacy batch or time-sharing operating systems inside virtual machines managed by hypervisors. If you want to explore further, research real-time patches for Linux like PREEMPT_RT and micro-kernel designs used in modern automotive operating systems like QNX.
